items.title: One 92 eV photon, 3,300 species, and a map of where the acid lands
items.dek: Nitesh Kumar and five co-authors traced what a single 92-electronvolt extreme-ultraviolet photon does inside a polymer photoresist — the light-sensitive film a chip pattern is printed into — following the cascade through more than 3,300 chemical species to a map of where reaction products end up.
items.why_it_matters: Every working model of resist behaviour starts by assuming which reactions matter, because nobody can enumerate them by hand. Searching millions of candidate reactions instead of guessing changes how a formulation gets judged: the paper finds that which molecule is ionised first, rather than how much energy the film absorbed, governs the downstream balance between deprotection and crosslinking — so absorbed dose on its own does not predict what a resist will do.
items.background_md: A photoresist turns light into a pattern by changing solubility where it is exposed, so the developer washes one region away and leaves the other. At 13.5 nm each extreme-ultraviolet photon carries about 92 eV, far more than any chemical bond, so it does not gently excite a molecule — it ionises one, and the ejected photoelectron scatters through the film making more low-energy electrons inside a small volume called a spur. The acids, radicals and fragments that decide whether a given nanometre dissolves are made by that cascade, not by the photon itself.
items.deeper_md:
The workflow runs in four stages: high-throughput density-functional theory over candidate species, automated reaction-network construction with a chemical-plausibility filter, stochastic sampling to pick out the pathways likely to carry flux, and spatially resolved reaction-diffusion kinetics that track species in space and time. Applied to an organic polymer resist it starts from over 3,300 species and millions of candidate reactions and returns product maps over femtosecond-to-nanosecond timescales across a 15.5 nm domain — roughly the size of the spur, and roughly the size of the features being printed, which is why the spatial part rather than the bulk kinetics is the point.

A separate group measuring pentafluorophenyl triflate at the same 92 eV found the parent ion at 3.1 percent of signal, CF₃⁺ dominant, and no dissociation channel yielding a triflic-acid precursor: a photoacid generator that absorbs EUV well and produces almost no acid. The two results point the same way about dose.

The caveat is that no wafer was printed. The simulations reproduce products detected experimentally, but no quantitative comparison against a measured dose-versus-roughness curve is claimed, and the plausibility filter that decides which of millions of reactions are chemically reasonable is itself a modelling assumption nobody outside the group has audited.

glossary.definition: The 13.5 nm radiation used to print the finest chip layers; each photon carries about 92 eV, so exposure proceeds by ionisation and electron cascades rather than the gentle bond excitation older resists were designed around.
The additive whose job is to release a strong acid on exposure; that acid then catalyses many solubility-switching reactions, which is where a chemically amplified resist gets its sensitivity.
The acid-catalysed removal of a blocking group from the polymer, turning an insoluble side chain into a soluble one — the reaction that makes an exposed region dissolve in developer.
The few-nanometre volume around an ionisation event in which the ejected electron dumps its energy, leaving a locally dense and spatially uneven cloud of reactive fragments.

items.fab_angle: A contrast curve measures a resist as a black box: dose in, thickness remaining out. This is the layer underneath it, and the claim is that two films with the same dose-to-clear can still behave differently because of which species the first ionisation happened to hit.

items.title: Write the waveguide in one pass, then cleave the chip with a diamond pen
items.dek: Kishor Kumar Mandal and seven co-authors wrote 500-nanometre silicon-nitride waveguides across a 5-millimetre chip as one unbroken electron-beam exposure, then cut the chips out by scoring the silicon with a diamond pen, getting end facets within 2° of normal on 80 percent of them.
items.why_it_matters: Scattering from a rough waveguide wall grows as the roughness variance divided by the fourth power of the guide dimension, so in a tightly confining air-clad guide a single misregistration where two exposure fields meet is not a small extra loss — it can set the loss budget by itself. Writing the whole device in one continuous motion removes that seam rather than shrinking it, and scribing instead of sawing leaves the open top surface the design exists to provide.
items.background_md: Light is held in an integrated waveguide by a step in refractive index, and the harder the index contrast the more of the mode presses against the etched sidewall. Roughness on that wall scatters light out of the guide, and the penalty grows sharply as the guide narrows, which is why a high-confinement circuit working at visible wavelengths is judged on wall quality rather than on material absorption. Electron-beam tools expose in fields a few hundred micrometres across and move the stage between them, so any device longer than one field carries a stitching boundary at every join.
items.deeper_md:
The platform is PECVD-grown Si₃N₄ with an air cladding, deliberately left uncovered so an externally placed emitter can reach the evanescent tail of the mode along the whole device length. Two process choices make that geometry survive at chip scale. Fixed-beam moving-stage electron-beam lithography exposes the 500 nm single-mode guide as one continuous write across the 5 mm chip, removing write-field stitching which, the authors argue, would otherwise dominate the loss budget at 635 nm given the σ²/d⁴ scaling of sidewall scattering in this geometry. Singulation is a pen-type diamond scribe run along lithographically patterned markers registered to the in-plane crystal direction, cleaving the Si(100) substrate; facets come out within 2° of normal at 80 percent yield.

What is reported is structural: SEM confirming stitch-free guides and undamaged near-vertical facets, end-fire coupling into a microring with bus-to-ring evanescent coupling confirmed by scattering imaging, and a roughness-dependent scattering model indicating loss stays low in that regime. What is not reported is a cutback measurement in dB/cm. For scale, a wafer-scale study that did measure, fitting SEM-extracted sidewall profiles to the Payne model, reported 0.075 dB/cm at 633 nm.

glossary.definition: The seam left where an electron-beam tool finishes one deflection field, moves the stage, and starts the next; the two exposures register to each other only as well as the stage does.
The part of a guided optical mode that extends outside the waveguide core and decays exponentially; anything placed within that reach — an emitter, another waveguide — couples to the light.
Sidewall scattering loss rises with the square of the roughness amplitude and falls with the fourth power of the guide dimension, so shrinking a high-contrast guide punishes wall quality very fast.
Breaking a silicon wafer along its natural crystal planes after scoring it, which produces a flat mirror-quality end face without the grinding and polishing a saw cut would need.

items.fab_angle: This is the failure mode a maskless stepper inherits by construction: every field boundary is a place where two separate exposures have to agree to within the tolerance the pattern cares about. MNF's tool will meet it as stitching between DMD frames, and the answer taken here — keep the stage moving and never stop the beam — removes the boundary instead of measuring it.

items.title: Tin leaves SiGeSn through the surface, so the fix is to cap the surface
items.dek: Anis Attiaoui and four co-authors watched silicon-germanium-tin films come apart under a 550 °C anneal and found the tin escapes through the free surface rather than the bulk: an ultrathin oxide cap held the composition to within one atomic percent while an uncapped film lost 60 percent of its thickness.
items.why_it_matters: If a metastable alloy decomposes from the surface inward, the remedy is a kinetic barrier on that surface rather than a lower processing temperature, and the distinction decides whether these films can survive a contact anneal at all. Capped films came out with contact resistivity twenty-five times lower than annealed uncapped ones, which is the gap between a layer that exists and a layer you can wire up.
items.background_md: Silicon and germanium are indirect-gap semiconductors and make poor light emitters, which is why photonics on a silicon wafer usually means bonding a III-V laser on top. Alloying tin into germanium pulls the band structure toward a direct gap and pushes emission past 2 µm, giving a group-IV gain material that a CMOS line can grow itself. The catch is that these alloys hold far more tin than equilibrium allows: they are metastable, and every later hot step is an opportunity for the tin to leave the lattice and form its own phase.
items.deeper_md:
The measurement is in situ spectroscopic ellipsometry run during an isothermal 550 °C anneal, so decomposition is watched as it happens rather than reconstructed from a cooled sample. Uncapped Si₀.₀₈Ge₀.₈₃Sn₀.₀₄ phase-separates after 50 minutes, with void formation, a 60 percent thickness reduction and a 400 meV blueshift of the E₂ critical point. The shift is the evidence: E₂ moves with substitutional tin content, so losing tin from the probed volume moves the optical signature. With an ultrathin oxide cap over the same 50 minutes, composition changes by under 1 at.% Sn and the optical shift stays under 20 meV, with void formation, strain relaxation and decomposition all suppressed. Contact resistivity falls 25-fold against the annealed uncapped film.

The same group's 2021 laser-annealing work had already seen tin segregate toward the surface and form columnar structures, with about an order of magnitude of contact-resistance improvement at the highest fluence. What is new is the claim that the surface route is the dominant one — and it rests on one composition at one temperature, with no device, no demonstration that the stability survives a full integration flow, and no independent repeat.

glossary.definition: A crystal holding more of one element than equilibrium permits, kept there by kinetics alone; heat gives the excess atoms the mobility to leave, so the alloy has a time-at-temperature budget rather than a melting point.

The cumulative time-at-temperature a wafer can absorb before structures already built are damaged — here the constraint that limits which contact and back-end steps a tin-bearing film can be put through.

A feature in a semiconductor's dielectric function at an energy where bands run parallel over a large region of the Brillouin zone; its position tracks alloy composition, which is why ellipsometry can read tin content optically.

The resistance per unit area of the metal-to-semiconductor interface, in Ω·cm²; it is set by barrier height and doping at the surface, and it dominates device resistance once the semiconductor itself is thin.

items.title: A multiply-accumulate in one cycle, because the adder was already there
items.dek: Yi Sheng Chong and four co-authors taped out a 40-nanometre reconfigurable processor array whose cells finish a multiply-accumulate in a single cycle by reusing the adder already inside the multiplier, and measured 420.6 giga-operations per second per watt at 0.6 volts.
items.why_it_matters: A coarse-grained reconfigurable array normally spends two cycles and two cells on a multiply-accumulate, because the product has to be routed onward to a separate adder, and in these arrays fetching and routing cost more energy than the arithmetic. Folding the accumulate into the multiplier's own final adder cuts instruction-memory accesses by 54 percent and drops the energy of a multiply-accumulate to 34 percent of the two-cycle version; the bill is a 3.2 nanosecond path, 1.86 times the multiplier alone.
items.background_md: A coarse-grained reconfigurable array is a grid of word-width arithmetic cells joined by a programmable network and reconfigured per kernel: coarser than an FPGA, which routes individual bits and takes a long time to load, and more flexible than a fixed-function accelerator. The recurring cost is that each cell executes one operation per cycle out of its own instruction memory, so any computation that does not fit a single cell's function spends a second cell and a network hop to finish. Operand movement and configuration fetch, not multiplication, set the energy.
items.deeper_md:
The array is 8 × 8 cells over 64 kB of data memory, mesh-connected to four neighbours, with a RISC-V core handling control; a cell occupies 0.019 mm² in 40 nm CMOS. The multiplier and adder inside a cell are shared, so the same hardware issues an add, a multiply, or a fused multiply-accumulate in one cycle depending on the instruction. Dynamic truncation is the other half: a 2-bit field selects between FXP⟨8,8⟩, FXP⟨4,12⟩ and FXP⟨2,14⟩ fixed-point formats, with boundary checks that saturate to the maximum value on overflow rather than wrapping around.

Measured silicon gives 47.6 mW average at 1 V, and 420.6 GOPS/W at 0.6 V and 21 MHz, which the authors place 1.4× above the best of seven prior designs. That headline number wants reading carefully. It is taken at a supply and a clock far below the 100 MHz design target, where dynamic energy per operation is near its minimum, so it is an energy-per-operation figure and not a throughput figure. The workload is general matrix multiply, the friendliest possible case for a fused multiply-accumulate, and efficiency comparisons across different process nodes and supply voltages are not like for like.

glossary.definition: An array of word-width arithmetic cells wired by a programmable network, reconfigured per kernel rather than per bit — it trades an FPGA's fine-grained flexibility for far less configuration memory and much lower reconfiguration time.
The operation a·b + c, the inner loop of matrix multiply and convolution; how many cycles and how much routing one costs is what mostly determines an accelerator's efficiency.

Billions of operations per second per watt — energy per operation expressed upside down. It rises when a chip is slowed and its supply lowered, so it must always be quoted with the voltage and clock it was measured at.

A 16-bit fixed-point format with 8 integer and 8 fractional bits; moving the binary point trades range against resolution at constant width, which is why a runtime-selectable split is worth the two bits it costs.

items.title: Hammer the aggressor rows harder than the decoys and GPU ECC folds
items.dek: Chris S. Lin, Joyce Qu, Aditya Rajeev and Gururaj Saileshwar released GPUThor, a Rowhammer attack that pounds aggressor rows far harder than decoy rows and flips up to 23,597 GDDR6 bits per memory bank on Nvidia workstation GPUs — enough that some triple-bit errors pass the card's error-correcting code as clean data.
items.why_it_matters: The code on these parts corrects one error and detects two across each 16 bytes, so three flips inside one 16-byte chunk can produce the same syndrome as a single flip elsewhere: the controller corrects the wrong bit, logs nothing, and returns corrupted data. Going from tens of flips per bank to tens of thousands is what turns that coincidence from an arithmetic curiosity into a working exploit, which is why the fix has to be a stronger code rather than a higher disturbance threshold.
items.background_md: A DRAM bit is charge on a capacitor, read destructively and rewritten on every refresh. Activating one row over and over disturbs its neighbours — charge leaks and couples across the array — so bits flip in rows the attacker never addressed, which is Rowhammer. Manufacturers answer inside the DRAM with target row refresh, sampling activations and refreshing likely victims early. That defence is budgeted against an assumed worst-case activation count per refresh window, so every attack on it is an argument about how many activations can be aimed at one row before the sampler notices.
items.deeper_md:
Three obstacles had to fall. GPUs coalesce repeated accesses within a warp, so hammering one address in a loop produces a single activation; the answer is to spread accesses at least 128 bytes apart across several warps inside the same row. The in-DRAM mitigation had been assumed to act once per refresh interval, but measuring multi-tREFI patterns showed it acting roughly every 72 tREFI, which leaves room for a six-tREFI pattern delivering 6.6 aggressor activations per interval, about 110,000 per refresh window, against a first-flip threshold of 12,300 to 15,800 activations.

The result is 14,311 flips per bank on an RTX A6000 where last year's GPUHammer from the same group managed 2.0, and 23,597 on an A5000 — 377,552 per gigabyte, approaching the 550,000 per gigabyte Blacksmith reaches on DDR4. Privilege escalation drops from 7 to 21.9 hours down to 0.6 to 1.2 minutes.

Limits the authors state themselves: only GA10x GDDR6 parts reproduced, while HBM, GDDR6X and newer GDDR6 did not; and only the locally owned A6000 could be tested with ECC switched on, because the cloud providers hosting the other three would not permit it.

glossary.definition: Flipping bits in a DRAM row you never addressed, by activating a physically adjacent row often enough that leakage and coupling drain the victim cells before the next refresh restores them.
Single-error-correcting, double-error-detecting code — enough redundancy to repair one wrong bit in a protected chunk and to notice two, and no defence at all once three go wrong together.
The average interval between DRAM refresh commands, tens of microseconds; it is the clock that both the refresh schedule and the in-DRAM Rowhammer mitigation are budgeted against.

A mitigation inside the DRAM that samples which rows are being activated heavily and refreshes their neighbours early; it is proprietary, undocumented, and defeated by patterns its sampler was not designed for.

items.title: Seekable compression costs 1.6 percent, or 6.6, depending on the format
items.dek: Yakiv Shavidze measured the density you give up to make compressed data seekable: cutting a 254-megabyte archive into independently addressable 16-kibibyte units costs 1.632 percent of the archive in an absolute-offset format against 6.57 percent for seekable zstd, and 5.33 against 10.06 percent at 4 kibibytes.
items.why_it_matters: LZ77-family compression works by pointing backwards into bytes already decoded, so any chunk you want to read on its own must begin with that history discarded, and the matches thrown away are what you pay. Knowing the exchange rate settles design choices usually made by habit: at 1.6 percent you can split an archive, append to it without a format change, and let a CPU and a GPU decoder share one file, and at 6.6 percent you cannot.
items.background_md: A general-purpose compressor replaces a repeated run of bytes with a reference back to where that run appeared earlier, so decoding byte N can require having already decoded a byte tens of thousands of positions behind it. That makes decompression inherently sequential and random access awkward: to jump into the middle of a file, a format has to reset its back-reference history at known points, and each reset throws away every match that would have crossed it. Block size is therefore a direct trade between how finely you can seek and how well the data compresses.
items.deeper_md:
The comparison covers four formats along nine axes on one corpus, a 254 MB archive. Absolute-offset addressing costs 1.632 percent of the archive at 16 KiB granularity and 5.33 percent at 4 KiB; seekable zstd costs 6.57 and 10.06 percent for the same units. The published seekable-format specification shows the gap is not bookkeeping: its seek table is a single skippable frame at the end of the file carrying one 8- or 12-byte entry per frame, which at 16 KiB units works out to well under a tenth of a percent. Almost all of the 6.57 percent is therefore compression lost at frame boundaries — each frame restarts with an empty window and, per RFC 8478, with the repeat-offset history reset to its defaults of 1, 4 and 8.

Three structural claims come with proofs and bit-perfect verification: that the repeat-distance chain of an LZ77 parse forms a substitution monoid and is therefore prefix-scannable without touching the bitstream, that self-overlapping matches are periodic rather than chained, and that dependency depth admits an encoder-enforced bound. Splitting a tiled archive measured at −0.28 percent, meaning slightly smaller after the split.

One author, one corpus, no venue, and nobody has rerun the measurements.

glossary.definition: The compression idea underneath gzip, zstd and almost everything else: emit a repeated byte run as a (distance, length) pair pointing into output already produced, which makes decoding cheap but strictly sequential.
A small cache of the most recently used match distances that a compressor can refer to in one or two bits instead of re-encoding the full distance; resetting it at a block boundary costs real bits.
An index appended to a compressed file listing each independently decodable frame's compressed and decompressed size, so a reader can compute a byte offset and jump without scanning.
1,024 bytes, as opposed to the kB of 1,000 bytes; block-size arguments in storage are always in binary units because they have to line up with page and sector boundaries.

items.title: Bitwise-reproducible training exists, and it costs most of the throughput
items.dek: A Gensyn team led by John Donaghy trained Open-1B, a 1.61-billion-parameter language model whose 80,957 optimiser steps can each be replayed on different hardware and hashed to identical bits, and reported that the fixed arithmetic ordering this requires costs most of the training throughput.
items.why_it_matters: Floating-point addition is not associative, so summing the same gradients in a different order changes the last bits, and across eighty thousand steps that becomes a different model — which is why publishing weights, data and code still does not let anyone verify that a released checkpoint came from the released recipe. Pinning the reduction order turns that verification into a hash comparison, and this is the first public price tag on it: reproducible bf16 ran at 3.3 percent model FLOPs utilisation against PyTorch's 40.5.
items.background_md: A floating-point number carries a fixed number of significand bits, so adding a small quantity to a large one discards part of the small one, and the answer depends on the order the additions happened in. Training is one very long chain of such sums spread across many devices, each reducing its partial results in whatever order its kernels find fastest, and that order changes with the shape of the cluster. Two runs of identical code on identical data therefore diverge, which is why reproducibility in machine learning is normally defined as agreement within a tolerance rather than equality.
items.deeper_md:
Open-1B is 1.61 B parameters, 1.08 B of them outside the embedding, a 24-layer decoder at hidden size 2,048, trained on 400 B tokens of 4,096-token sequences over 80,957 steps on 48 H100s across six eight-GPU nodes, 27.8 days of active training inside 29.5 calendar days.

Determinism is not one fix but seven. A library called RepOps pins reduction order; multiply-add fusion is disabled on CPUs and written out explicitly on GPUs so both round the same way; subnormal handling is matched to the strictest backend; randomness comes from a counter-based Philox generator keyed to seed and logical position rather than to call order; the data stream is made invariant to cluster topology; and collectives use a recursive-doubling butterfly all-reduce with an ascending-order reduce-scatter.

The bill: reproducible int8 quantisation-aware training reached 42.1k tokens/s against PyTorch's 288k, and reproducible bf16 3.3 percent MFU against 40.5. That bought 400 B tokens where OLMo 2 had 4 T, and 25.4 on OLMES against 31.9. Per-step state hashing adds about 6 seconds, roughly 2 percent of a step. The audit proves the declared recipe was followed; it says nothing about whether the declared data was worth training on.

glossary.definition: (a+b)+c ≠ a+(b+c) in floating point, because each addition rounds; it is the reason the same arithmetic on the same data gives different last bits when the order changes.
A single instruction computing a·b + c with one rounding instead of two; it is faster and more accurate, and it makes a fused and an unfused machine disagree in the last bit.
The collective that sums a tensor across every device and gives all of them the result; the order it adds the contributions in is normally chosen for speed and varies with topology.

The fraction of a machine's peak arithmetic throughput a training run actually converts into useful model FLOPs; 40 percent is a healthy number and 3.3 percent means the hardware is idle most of the time.

foundations.subtitle: Four pages in a trade magazine, an argument about manufacturing cost rather than physics, and a straight line drawn through five points.
foundations.tldr: In April 1965 Gordon Moore, then running research at Fairchild Semiconductor, wrote four pages in Electronics magazine arguing that the cheapest way to buy a given amount of electronics keeps moving toward putting more components on one chip. The famous doubling was five data points and a ten-year extrapolation hung on that argument, not the argument itself. Read the paper for the cost curve and the doubling stops looking like a law of nature and starts looking like a claim about yield.

sections.heading: The thesis is sitting in the subtitle
sections.body_md:
The Computer History Museum's catalogue record for the article gives its full title line, and it is the whole paper compressed: "With unit cost falling as the number of components per circuit rises, by 1975 economics may dictate squeezing as many as 65,000 components on a single silicon chip."

Read that again, because almost every later retelling drops the first clause. The claim is not that 65,000 components will become physically possible. It is that 65,000 will become the *cheapest* number — that economics will dictate it. Moore was Director of Research and Development Laboratories at Fairchild Semiconductor at the time, writing for an anniversary issue of a trade magazine, and his job was to persuade electronics engineers that integrated circuits were about to stop being a specialty part. The argument he chose was about cost per function, because that was the only argument his audience cared about. The exponential curve is the evidence, not the conclusion.
sections.deeper_md: The article ran in Electronics, Vol. 38, No. 8, dated 19 April 1965, and is four pages long. It is worth knowing that Moore had made a version of the argument the year before, in a Fairchild document titled "The Future of Integrated Electronics" (1964), which the museum lists alongside it. The 1965 piece also ranges much wider than the doubling curve — it discusses power dissipation, linear as well as digital circuits, and the limits of photolithography — and Moore returned to that last theme thirty years later in "Lithography and the Future of Moore's Law" at SPIE in 1995.

sections.heading: Why cost per component has a minimum at all
sections.body_md:
Here is the mechanism the subtitle is pointing at. Put more components on a die and two things happen in opposite directions.

Everything charged per *chip* — the package, the handling, the test insertion, the assembly into a board — gets divided across more components, so that part of the cost per component falls as you add function. But the die also gets bigger, and a bigger die is more likely to swallow a defect. Model defects as randomly scattered at density D₀ and the chance a die of area A contains none of them is a Poisson exponential, Y = e^(−D₀A). That is not a gentle penalty: it is exponential in area, so past some point each extra square millimetre costs more in dead die than it buys in amortised packaging.

Add the two curves and you get a U. The bottom of the U is a specific number of components, and that number is what Moore plotted. As process control improves and D₀ falls, the exponential relaxes and the bottom of the U slides toward more components per chip. The doubling curve is the trajectory of that minimum.
sections.deeper_md: Do the arithmetic to feel the exponent. The University of Pennsylvania's CIS 501 problem set uses a 300 mm wafer costing $25,000 with a defect density of 1 per 500 mm², i.e. 0.002 defects/mm², and asks for yield at die areas of 100, 200 and 400 mm². Under Y = e^(−D₀A) that is e^(−0.2) ≈ 0.82, e^(−0.4) ≈ 0.67 and e^(−0.8) ≈ 0.45. Doubling the die twice does not halve the yield — it costs you nearly half of what remains, twice. The plain Poisson form is the optimistic model, too: real fabs fit Murphy or negative-binomial distributions, which allow defects to cluster and give higher yields at large areas than the exponential predicts.

sections.heading: Five points and a straight line
sections.body_md:
The evidence in the paper is thinner than its reputation. Writing in IEEE Spectrum in 2015, Chris Mack describes what Moore actually plotted: five points over time, beginning with Fairchild's first planar transistor and continuing through a series of the company's integrated circuit offerings, on a semilogarithmic axis where an exponential appears as a straight line. The line through them corresponded to a doubling of components per chip every year. The Computer History Museum dates those minimum-cost points to 1959 through 1964.

From five points spanning roughly five years, Moore extrapolated ten. That is the daring part, and it is the part that would get a referee's attention in any other field. It also landed: Mack notes the 65,000 projection came close to the memory chips of around 32,000 components that were actually shipping a decade later.

The habit worth taking from this is not "trust exponentials". It is that Moore knew what mechanism was driving his line, so he knew what would have to keep being true for the extrapolation to hold.
sections.deeper_md: A semilog plot is doing real work here and is easy to abuse. On linear-log axes any process with a constant fractional growth rate is a straight line, and the eye reads straightness as confirmation — but the same eye cannot distinguish a true exponential from a logistic curve until the logistic is well past its inflection point. Five points is not enough to tell them apart. What made Moore's extrapolation defensible was not the fit quality but the causal story underneath it: he could name the thing that moved the cost minimum, and he could see no reason for it to stop within ten years.

sections.heading: What the 1975 revision actually said
sections.body_md:
Ten years on, at the IEEE International Electron Devices Meeting, Moore revisited the projection. The interesting content is the decomposition. As Mack summarises it, Moore attributed the growth in components per chip to three separate contributors: components getting smaller, chips getting bigger, and what Moore called device cleverness — designers finding and eliminating wasted space in the layout. Roughly half the doubling came from the first two; roughly half came from cleverness.

That split is why the rate changed. Shrinking and growing the die are renewable: each new generation of lithography and each larger wafer buys another increment. Cleverness is not. Once you have removed the empty space from a memory cell, you cannot remove it again. Moore's revised figure — a doubling every two years instead of every year — is, read this way, not a pessimistic mood. It is an arithmetic consequence of taking one of the three contributors out of the sum.

Every later statement that "Moore's Law is eighteen months" or "two years" is arguing about a number Moore himself only ever derived from this decomposition.
sections.deeper_md: The 1975 talk was published as "Progress in Digital Integrated Electronics" in the IEDM Technical Digest, pp. 11–13, and it is short. Note what the decomposition implies about the difference between memory and logic: memory arrays are regular, so cleverness is exhausted early and reliably, while logic keeps finding layout savings for longer. Mack notes Moore's revised rate proved accurate specifically for logic chips such as microprocessors, which were less dense than memory of the same generation — the two curves were never the same curve.

sections.heading: Three things the paper never claimed
sections.body_md:
First, it says nothing about speed. The idea that chips get faster every generation is Dennard scaling, published nine years later and describing a completely different mechanism — shrink the dimensions and the voltage together and power density holds constant. When that broke around the 100 nm generation, as leakage stopped the voltage from coming down, performance stopped tracking density even though density kept going. Two laws, two fates.

Second, it is not a law. Nothing in physics makes transistor counts double. What made the line straight for decades is that an industry adopted it as a schedule and coordinated to it: equipment vendors, materials suppliers and fabs each committed capital against a shared roadmap, which became the ITRS and, since 2016, the IEEE's IRDS.

Third, 65,000 was never a maximum. It was the cost-optimal count under the yield conditions Moore expected for 1975. A chip with more components than that was buildable; it just would not have been the cheapest way to buy the function.
sections.deeper_md: The roadmap point is the one that gets least attention and explains the most. A self-fulfilling prophecy is not a fake one: if a tool vendor believes the schedule and builds to it, and a fab believes the vendor and plans a node against it, the prophecy is what synchronised billions of dollars of unrelated capital spending. The IRDS at irds.ieee.org still publishes free editions on this model — 2024 and 2025 update and a 2026 edition are listed — which is what a coordination device looks like once nobody believes it is a natural law any more.

sections.heading: Reading it in 2026
sections.body_md:
The durable part of the 1965 paper is the U-curve, and it is the reason the current argument about chiplets is the same argument Moore was having. Once a die is large enough that the yield exponential dominates, and large enough to run into the size of field an exposure tool can print at once, the minimum-cost configuration stops being one big die and becomes several smaller ones bonded together. That is not a departure from Moore's reasoning. It is his reasoning applied to a defect density and a die area he did not have.

What has changed is that keeping the line straight now requires a new physical trick every few years rather than a steady shrink. David Lammers' Spectrum timeline lists the interventions: ion implantation from 1972, chemical mechanical planarization arriving with the Pentium in 1993, uniaxial strained silicon at 90 nm in 2002, FinFETs at 22 nm in 2011. Each of those was a one-time debt payment to keep an economic trend on schedule — which is exactly what you would expect if the trend was economic all along.
sections.deeper_md: Mack's framing is worth borrowing: a Moore's Law 1.0 about scaling *up*, putting more components on a chip, and a Moore's Law 2.0 about scaling *down*, shrinking and cheapening the transistor whatever the component count. He argues a 3.0 is now underway, about integrating functions that are not logic — analogue, RF, photonics, memory — onto or into one package. Note that 3.0 has no guaranteed cost trajectory attached to it. Integrating a photodiode and a processor makes a better product; it does not automatically make either one cheaper per function, which is what the original curve was about.

glossary.definition: Killer defects per unit area on a wafer, typically quoted in defects/cm². It is the single number that connects process cleanliness to how large a die you can afford to build.

Y = e^(−D₀A): the probability that a die of area A contains zero randomly placed defects. It is the simplest useful yield model and deliberately pessimistic at large areas, because real defects cluster rather than scattering independently.
In Moore's article, any circuit element on the chip — transistor, resistor, diode — not specifically a transistor. The later habit of quoting transistor counts is a different, larger number.
One axis linear, the other logarithmic, so any constant fractional growth rate draws as a straight line. It makes exponentials legible and makes logistic curves look exponential until quite late.

Moore's own 1975 term for layout and circuit improvements that raise component count without any change in feature size or die area — squeezing out wasted space. He treated it as a contributor that would run out, and it did.

The International Roadmap for Devices and Systems, the IEEE successor to the ITRS since 2016: the industry's shared schedule for what has to work by when, and the institutional form Moore's Law eventually took.

foundations.try_this: Rebuild Moore's cost curve yourself this week. Use the AnySilicon die-per-wafer calculator to get gross die on a 300 mm wafer for a range of die areas, pair it with Y = e^(−D₀A) and the die-cost arithmetic in the Penn CIS 501 problem set ($25,000 per wafer, D₀ = 0.002 defects/mm², die areas of 100, 200 and 400 mm²), and plot cost per component against components per die for two defect densities an order of magnitude apart. The minimum of that curve is the entire 1965 paper; watch how far right it slides when you drop D₀. Then read the yield chapter of Van Zant's Microchip Fabrication and work out which of its defect models the plain exponential is the pessimistic one against, and by how much at 400 mm².
